title: Why Stripe is not what you need to charge for your AI product (kind of)
summary:
Like everyone else, you build a product and need to charge your customers. Your first instinct is to go to Stripe. Stripe is the GOAT, so of course you'll use it.

This is true and untrue, let's say you're building an AI product. You probably won't charge your customers a flat monthly fee that covers all usage as they have a really different cost for your business depending on how they use your product. Instead, you might want to have pricing based on usage. Sounds good. Stripe covers that, case closed... Well, yes and no. There are two types of usage-based billing. One lets customers use the product and pay later, which exposes your business to unpaid bills, and we don't want that... The other uses credits purchased up front.

Credits are what most businesses are moving toward nowadays. They give security on both sides, for the business and the customer. They also show you not only how your customers use your product but more importantly how they spend in your product.

So you're sold on credits, great, let's set them up in Stripe. This is where things start to get complicated. There's a new account system to figure out, confusion between usage-based billing and credits, meters to set up, and that one credits tab to find in Stripe's whole suite of products to monitor them. Then you have to make sure all the pieces work together, figure out how to keep your customers' credit balances in sync. Oh, and if you want to calculate your margin on every credit spent... good luck...

It's doable, but far from trivial. It is similar to deploying your app on Vercel in a minute versus taking a course on how to deploy on AWS and rearchitect your whole app to match AWS architecture. You have better things to do, right? You're building an AI product, not a credit system. You want an abstraction layer on top that makes your life easier, not harder.

By now, I hope you're convinced there's an easier way (even if your agent does most of the work). If you've used something like Vercel, it's hard to imagine going back to DevOps and the low-level infrastructure of AWS. This is where a platform built for credits makes sense. It handles a lot of those architectural decisions for you so you don't have to stitch everything together yourself, losing a bit of confidence with every stitch. You want to know which features customers spend their credits on, how much each of those features cost you and if your margin are protected even if you give away promotional credits.

Of course, managing credits and taking payments for them are two different jobs. You still want an established solution for payments, and Stripe is the best at that. That's why this credit layer and payment solution should work together and integrate all the best things from Stripe.

That's what we're building with https://orbytelabs.com. We've built credit systems too many times and taken too many shortcuts in the past that came back to hurt the business later. We want to do for credits what Vercel did for application deployment. Keep the power of Stripe without having to deal with the complexity of building your own credit infrastructure.

title: Ask HN: Do coding harnesses not have prompt queue management features?
summary:
Hey HN,

I find myself in this situation almost daily:

- I have some long-running task in my session going - I queue up a few more prompts as that task is running, in the same session. - I realize I want to to edit, re-order, delete or consolidate one of those several queued prompts

I'm surprised to not find intuitive and seamless support for this workflow. I use github copilot CLI as my daily driver (MSFT employee), but I have tried claude code, opencode and other harnesses as well. I realize I could start another /session , but often times the queued prompts build upon eachother or the currently running task, so it makes more sense to be able to edit them and wait for the current work to be done.

I'm imagining a /queue command that brings up a TUI list of the queued prompts, or perhaps a vim window with all of them and you can edit them in a similar way to how you do "git rebase -i" and pick/squash git commits if that makes sense.

Perhaps some of the more GUI harnesses have better queue management.

How are you handling this scenario?

Thanks, Happy thanksgiving!

title: DietPi released a new version v10.9
summary:
DietPi is a lightweight Debian based Linux distribution for SBCs and server systems, with the option to install desktop environments, too. It ships as minimal image but allows to install complete and ready-to-use software stacks with a set of console based shell dialogs and scripts.

The source code is hosted on GitHub: https://github.com/MichaIng/DietPi The main website can be found at: https://dietpi.com/ Wikipedia: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/DietPi

The project released the version DietPi v10.9 on November 21st, 2026.

The highlights of this version are:

Odroid C5, Orange Pi 6/6 Plus, Orange Pi Zero 4, Orange Pi 4A: New supported SBCs Paperless-ngx: New software package: Document management system Yuvomi: New software package: Self-hosted family planner SolidPing: New software package: Uptime monitoring tool Podman: New software package: Daemonless container engine (Docker compatible) Readarr, Mono: Removed software packages (outdated) DietPi-Fan_control: New tool, configure temperature-controlled cooling fans on Raspberry Pi Enhancements for Quartz64, Odroid C2, dietpi-banner, dietpi-cloudshell, dietpi-vpn, dietpi-network, dietpi-software, Node.js, Node-RED Fixes for UTM-VMs, dietpi-banner, dietpi-vpn, dietpi-network, dietpi-wireguard, dietpi-software The full release notes can be found at: https://dietpi.com/docs/releases/v10_9/

event_model_payload.summary:
Happy Thanksgiving!

This question crossed my mind in the morning. It feels like I have seen pretty much everything under the Sun. I have modest house (still renting), small kids, a okayish job. I spent time on daily activities and occassionally on long walks.

The progress with AI and impact on Software is frankly exciting and depressing at the same time.

What are people my age doing these days? How do you keep yourself excited for the future and not feel anxious?

Curious to see from a bit older people here how are you doing and challenging yourself well into 40s, 50s and 60s.
